"'''I Wanna Sex You Up'''" is a song by American [[contemporary R&B|R&B]] group [[Color Me Badd]], released in March 1991 as the [[lead single]] from their debut album, ''[[C.M.B.]]'' (1991). The song was produced by [[Dr. Freeze]] and was also featured on the [[New Jack City (soundtrack)|soundtrack]] to the 1991 film ''[[New Jack City]]'', starring [[Wesley Snipes]], [[Ice-T]], [[Chris Rock]] and [[Judd Nelson]]. The song heavily samples "Tonight Is the Night" by [[Betty Wright]].{{citation needed|date=March 2025}}

The single, released by [[Giant Records (Warner)|Giant]] and [[Reprise Records]], achieved commercial success in the United States, spending four weeks at number two on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and topping both the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Hot R&B Singles]] and [[12-inch Singles Sales]] charts. "I Wanna Sex You Up" also experienced international success, peaking atop the charts of New Zealand and the United Kingdom. The accompanying music video was directed by American director [[Lionel C. Martin]].<ref>{{cite web|first=Darren|last=Jamison|title=100 Greatest Popular Songs of the 1990s|publisher=singersroom.com|date=March 1, 2023|access-date=February 16, 2024|url=https://singersroom.com/content/2023-03-01/100-greatest-popular-songs-of-the-1990s/}}</ref>

"I Wanna Sex You Up" is a song by American R&B group Color Me Badd, released in March 1991 as the lead single from their debut album, C.M.B. (1991). The song was produced by Dr. Freeze and was also featured on the soundtrack to the 1991 film New Jack City, starring Wesley Snipes, Ice-T, Chris Rock and Judd Nelson. The song heavily samples "Tonight Is the Night" by Betty Wright.{{citation needed|date=March 2025}}

The single, released by Giant and Reprise Records, achieved commercial success in the United States, spending four weeks at number two on the Billboard Hot 100 and topping both the Billboard Hot R&B Singles and 12-inch Singles Sales charts. "I Wanna Sex You Up" also experienced international success, peaking atop the charts of New Zealand and the United Kingdom. The accompanying music video was directed by American director Lionel C. Martin.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: A reviewer from ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' described the song as "naughty and suggestive yet not particularly explicit [[R&B-Pop|R&B/pop]]".<ref>{{cite magazine|title= Pop Reviews: Singles |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]] |date= April 27, 1991 |page= 5 |access-date= October 31, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/90s/1991/CB-1991-04-27.pdf}}</ref> Arion Berger from ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' complimented it as "irresistible".<ref>Berger, Arion (August 9, 1991). "C.M.B.". ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''.</ref> Dennis Hunt from ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' found that all it "has going for it is sexy lyrics."<ref>{{cite news|first=Dennis|last=Hunt|title=In Brief|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=September 15, 1991|page=|accessdate=January 22, 2023|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-09-15-ca-3486-story.html}}</ref> [[James Hamilton (DJ and journalist)|James Hamilton]] from ''[[Music Week]]'''s ''RM'' Dance Update called it a "sweetly cooing young guys crooned gorgeous sineous sexy swayer" in his weekly dance column.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= James |last= Hamilton |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/UK/Music-Week/1991/MW-1991-05-04.pdf |title= DJ Directory: Hot Vinyl |magazine= [[Music Week]], in [[Record Mirror]] (Dance Update Supplemental Insert) |date= May 4, 1991 |page= 6 |access-date= October 3, 2020 |author-link= James Hamilton (DJ and journalist)}}</ref> [[Stephen Holden]] from ''[[New York Times]]'' wrote, "'I Wanna Sex You Up' has a loping pop [[Latin music|Latin beat]] that is similar to [[the Young Rascals]]' '[[Groovin']]' and [[Laura Nyro]]'s '[[Stoned Soul Picnic (song)|Stoned Soul Picnic]]', and a piercing lead vocal by [[Bryan Abrams]], whose voice resembles that of the late-1960's [[Stevie Wonder]]."<ref>[[Stephen Holden|Holden, Stephen]] (May 8, 1991). "The Pop Life". ''[[New York Times]]''.</ref> [[David Fricke]] from ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' declared it as "a crafty blend of [[doo-wop]] doo-wah and [[Hip hop music|hip-hop]] clatter so irresistible it makes you willing to forgive the utter banality of the lyrics."<ref name="fricke"/> [[Mark Frith (journalist)|Mark Frith]] from ''[[Smash Hits]]'' felt that [[Color Me Badd]] "sound excellent" when "they do manage to break into a sweat", like on "I Wanna Sex You Up".<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Mark |last= Frith |title= Review: LPs |magazine= [[Smash Hits]] |date= August 7, 1991 |page= 46 |access-date= October 20, 2020 |url= https://www.flickr.com/photos/smashhits90s/31206939338/in/album-72157702019922435/ |author-link= Mark Frith (journalist)}}</ref>
sections.text: A reviewer from Cashbox described the song as "naughty and suggestive yet not particularly explicit R&B/pop". Arion Berger from Entertainment Weekly complimented it as "irresistible". Dennis Hunt from Los Angeles Times found that all it "has going for it is sexy lyrics." James Hamilton from Music Weeks RM Dance Update called it a "sweetly cooing young guys crooned gorgeous sineous sexy swayer" in his weekly dance column. Stephen Holden from New York Times wrote, "'I Wanna Sex You Up' has a loping pop Latin beat that is similar to the Young Rascals' 'Groovin and Laura Nyro's 'Stoned Soul Picnic', and a piercing lead vocal by Bryan Abrams, whose voice resembles that of the late-1960's Stevie Wonder." David Fricke from Rolling Stone declared it as "a crafty blend of doo-wop doo-wah and hip-hop clatter so irresistible it makes you willing to forgive the utter banality of the lyrics." Mark Frith from Smash Hits felt that Color Me Badd "sound excellent" when "they do manage to break into a sweat", like on "I Wanna Sex You Up".

sections.heading: Retrospective response
sections.wikitext: Alex Henderson from [[AllMusic]] named the song as one of the "moments" on the ''[[C.M.B.]]'' album, describing it as a slow jam which samples rapper [[Slick Rick]] "in a rather clever fashion".<ref>{{cite web|first= Alex |last= Henderson |title= Color Me Badd – ''C.M.B.'' |publisher= [[AllMusic]] |access-date= November 4, 2020 |url= https://www.allmusic.com/album/cmb-mw0000264421}}</ref> "I Wanna Sex You Up" was ranked number 40 on [[Blender (magazine)|''Blender'']]'s list of the "50 Worst Songs Ever"<ref>[http://www.blender.com/lists/61412/the50worstsongseverwatchlistenandcringe.html?p=3 The 50 Worst Songs Ever!  Watch, Listen and Cringe!] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101226224442/http://www.blender.com/lists/61412/the50worstsongseverwatchlistenandcringe.html?p=3 |date=December 26, 2010 }} from ''Blender.com''</ref> and [[VH1]]'s "100 Greatest Songs of the '90s".{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} In a 2017 retrospective review, Pop Rescue commented, "This song stood out from the rest of the charts when it was released in the UK, and that along with the boys’ breathy sexy promises and the inclusion of ‘sex’ in the song title made this track a sure-fire hit. Musically it's quite a simple song, allowing the vocals to really shine here – and to their credit, their vocals worth together really well."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://poprescue.com/2017/03/29/review-c-m-b-by-color-me-badd-1991-cd/|title=Review: "C. M. B" by Color Me Badd (CD, 1991)|publisher=Pop Rescue|date=March 29, 2017|access-date=October 4, 2020}}</ref>
sections.text: Alex Henderson from AllMusic named the song as one of the "moments" on the C.M.B. album, describing it as a slow jam which samples rapper Slick Rick "in a rather clever fashion". "I Wanna Sex You Up" was ranked number 40 on Blenders list of the "50 Worst Songs Ever" and VH1's "100 Greatest Songs of the '90s".{{citation needed|date=January 2022}} In a 2017 retrospective review, Pop Rescue commented, "This song stood out from the rest of the charts when it was released in the UK, and that along with the boys’ breathy sexy promises and the inclusion of ‘sex’ in the song title made this track a sure-fire hit. Musically it's quite a simple song, allowing the vocals to really shine here – and to their credit, their vocals worth together really well."

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: The song spent three weeks at number one on the [[UK Singles Chart]] and reached number two for four consecutive weeks on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]. It was the 10th-best-selling single of 1991 in the UK and the second-best-selling single of the year in the US. In 1992 the song won the group a [[Soul Train Music Award for Best R&B/Soul Single, Group, Band or Duo]] and [[Soul Train Music Award for Best R&B/Soul Song of the Year]].

In 1992 the song won the group a Soul Train Music Award for Best R&B/Soul Single, Group, Band or Duo and Soul Train Music Award for Best R&B/Soul Song of the Year.
